posts.quote: People are posting AI photos with flawless skin, flawless hair, and flawless bone structure. Then answering every compliment with “Aww, thank you.” Unbelievable.
posts.caption: A woman in my Zumba class posted a picture last week that I would have sworn was a Greek goddess on vacation. Same woman. I have watched her struggle with a water bottle lid. The comments poured in, all hearts and fire emojis, and she answered every one with the same sweet little thank you. I scrolled for a while. Then I looked at the photo I took of myself that morning, the one where my chin has a chin, and posted it anyway. Seventeen people liked it. Every one of them has seen me in person.
posts.first: My husband walked past while I was scrolling and asked who that was. I said it's Donna from Zumba. He squinted, said Donna doesn't look like that, and kept walking to the kitchen. That's the most honest review that photo will ever get. I liked it anyway. Manners.

posts.quote: I bought the sixty-eight dollar night cream. Three weeks in, the only thing glowing is my credit card statement.
posts.caption: It came in a little frosted jar with a tiny spoon-shaped scoop, which should have been my first warning. The woman at the department store counter called it a ritual and promised results in four weeks. I have been very faithful. Every night I stand at the bathroom mirror in the good light and apply it in small upward circles, like I'm polishing something expensive. In week three my husband said I looked tired. I told him it was working, that it was drawing the tiredness to the surface. He nodded like he'd read about it.
posts.first: The jar is almost empty now, which I've decided to count as progress. I went back to the counter on Saturday just to ask about the refill. The saleswoman remembered me and asked how my skin was doing. I said glowing. She said wonderful. I bought the refill. We both knew exactly what we were doing.

posts.quote: Honestly, is it just me? I can be starving, bloated, and gaining weight all at once. FFS.
posts.caption: I stood in front of the open pantry at 3:15 yesterday afternoon for what felt like a full minute. I wanted something salty, something sweet, and something crunchy, and I wanted none of it. My jeans, which fit on Sunday, have stopped returning my calls. I put a hand on my stomach and had a very serious talk with it. It did not listen. So I ate a handful of crackers standing up, and then I got mad at the crackers. None of that sequence made sense, and I'd do it again.
posts.first: At the checkout on Friday the girl asked if I wanted a bag for just the crackers. I said no, I'll carry them. I carried them to the car, sat in the parking lot, and ate six. She wasn't wrong to ask. I wasn't wrong to say no. We both left with our dignity mostly intact.

posts.quote: Every fall I swear I'll make homemade soup. By the third onion I'm crying, and the can opener is back in my hand.
posts.caption: Saturday morning I got out the big pot, the one that lives on the top shelf and only comes down when I'm feeling ambitious. I had a printed recipe with carrots, celery, and a bay leaf I'm not sure I've ever actually seen. The kitchen smelled wonderful for about fifteen minutes. Then the chopping got serious, my eyes gave out, and I noticed the radio had finished two whole songs while I was still on the vegetables. I stood there wiping my face with my elbow, having a quiet conversation with the pantry. The pantry had a plan.
posts.first: We ate it Saturday night, the canned one. My husband said it was the best soup I'd ever made. I didn't correct him. The big pot went back on the top shelf, and I wrote next fall on the recipe, circled it twice, and put it in the drawer with the other seven.

posts.quote: I picked up my phone to check the weather. Forty minutes later I'd watched a man in Ohio restore a rusty knife. I still don't know if it's raining.
posts.caption: It was a Tuesday morning and I had my coffee and one simple question. The weather app opened, and then somehow so did a video. The man in the video had a very calm voice and a bucket of something that dissolved rust, and I'd say I was nearly moved by the end. I learned a great deal about knife handles. When the timer on the stove finally went off, I realized the coffee had gone cold and I'd never once looked up. I went to the window instead. Gray. That was all the information I needed in the first place.
posts.first: I watched another one on the porch swing last week, different man, different knife. My husband asked what was so interesting and I told him I was learning a trade. He said at sixty-one? I said it's never too late. I still haven't touched a knife.

posts.quote: If you ever hear me say “I put it somewhere safe,” just go ahead and consider it lost forever.
posts.first: I hid my mother's good earrings in a coffee can in the garage in 2014. I was very proud of myself. It's now a decade later, and somewhere out there is a coffee can that knows exactly where they are. I'm not going to say I miss them. I'll say the garage has been very quiet about it.

posts.quote: Every now and then I meet someone and think, “Those eggs were definitely past their expiration date.”
posts.caption: There's a man in my building who corners me by the mailboxes. Every time. He always has a story about a guy he used to work with, and it never has an ending. Last Thursday it ran nine minutes. I counted on the lobby clock. I held my mail the whole time like a shield, and I think he took that as encouragement. I finally said I had something on the stove. I did not. I had a couch and a very strong need to be on it. It was a very good exit.
posts.first: He caught me again Monday. This time I took the stairs on the other side of the building and met him at the mailboxes anyway. He said what a coincidence. I said that's not the word I'd use. He laughed. He thought I was joking.

posts.quote: I used to need a night out to feel alive. Now I put on clean pajamas and feel like I won something.
posts.caption: Thursday evening I took a shower, dried off, and opened the drawer I'd been saving. The flannel set with the little snowflakes, still smelling like dryer sheets. I put them on slowly, one arm at a time. I'd turned the heat up two degrees and moved the throw blanket from the back of the couch to the front. By seven I was in my chair with a plate of cheese and crackers and the fireplace channel on. Nothing was on fire. It was glorious. I'd call it a perfect night out and I never left the house.
posts.first: My friend Joanne called around eight to ask if I wanted to try the new place downtown. I looked at my feet in their snowflake socks and told her I was already out. She asked where. I said the living room, in a manner of speaking. She hung up laughing. She understood.

posts.quote: I bought a matching workout set. I’ve worn it twice, both times to the grocery store. It’s thriving.
posts.caption: The saleswoman said the set would change my life. Leggings, a cropped top, a little zip jacket, all the same soft shade of sage. I tried it on in the fitting room and honestly looked like a woman with a trainer. I wore it to the grocery store that same afternoon, mostly so the tags wouldn't go to waste. Then again on Thursday. The sneakers still have the tissue paper in them. I'd like to say Monday is the day, but the set is thriving where it is, folded on the bench, looking hopeful.
posts.first: My sister asked how the workouts were going. I told her the outfit was doing very well. She asked if I'd actually exercised. I told her I'd carried two bags up the stairs in it, and she let that one go.

posts.quote: I told my doctor I walk every day. Technically true. It's mostly between the couch and the fridge.
posts.first: He wrote active on my chart and I watched him do it. The nurse asked how many steps a day. I said plenty, mostly diagonal. She didn't write that down. I'd like to think it's because she respected the answer.

posts.quote: We’ve officially entered “Put it on your Christmas list” season. Better known as “Stop asking me to buy stuff” season.
posts.caption: My sister-in-law texted at 8:03 Sunday morning asking for my Christmas list. It is October twentieth. She sent it to eleven people at once, so by lunch the whole family chain had turned into a catalog with opinions. Someone wanted socks. Someone wanted a gift card to the place with the good bread. I wanted to finish my coffee in peace. I typed a candle, probably, and sent it to all eleven by accident. By Monday morning four of them had a plan, and every one of those plans was a candle.
posts.first: I do like a candle. I would like to point out that I own nine of them and have never lit one. They sit on the shelf above the dryer like very expensive decorations. If the family wants to keep the tradition going, I'd gladly take a tenth.

posts.quote: Technology was supposed to save us time. Now I need the password I can’t remember and the verification code sent to the phone I can’t find.
posts.caption: At 9:10 Monday morning I sat down to pay one bill. One. The website said it didn't recognize me, which hurt. I tried the usual password, then the other usual password, then a third with an exclamation point I was fairly sure I'd invented in the shower. It sent a code to my phone. My phone was somewhere in the house, almost certainly on silent. I walked from room to room dialing it from the landline my husband refuses to cancel. It was in the fruit bowl, under the oranges. I'd love to say that was the end of it.
posts.first: The code expired while I was digging through the oranges. The website asked if I wanted to try again. I said not today. I mailed a check. It cost me a stamp and about ninety seconds, and I felt like a woman who had beaten the entire internet.
